own_scenes.place: Del Kemet a la Nave Nodriza
own_scenes.desc: Más que un estilo, una filosofía de vida que roza la religión: según Ashem Neru-Mesit, un «sistema de misterios» como los del antiguo Kemet, con ritos de paso. Clinton y Pedro Bell se burlaban de las doctrinas mientras creaban la suya: el «Swing down, sweet chariot» de «Mothership Connection» convertía el carro del himno en una nave con tripulación negra que volvía a reclamar las pirámides, poniendo la sensibilidad afroamericana en el centro del universo y de la historia. Una mitología negra postindustrial de ciencia ficción, en la que los blancos no existían: Star Child, Dr. Funkenstein y su enemigo Sir Nose D’Voidoffunk, que se niega a bailar y contagia el Placebo Syndrome; superhéroes animados a imagen de los niños negros que daban la vuelta a la asociación de negro con malo. Tras los derechos civiles, el éxodo hacia la Tierra Prometida se volvió el aterrizaje de la Nave en los estadios. «On the One» es la unidad cósmica africana de todo: «One Nation Under a Groove», «todo el mundo en el mismo pulso». La autosuperación («Free your mind and your ass will follow / The kingdom of heaven is within», «bailar bajo el agua sin mojarse» en «Aqua Boogie») y el equilibrio entre lo sagrado y lo profano («All that is good, is nasty!»): la fuerza vital única de la filosofía africana, el Ra kemético o la Kundalini, alcanzada por el trance extático. Ese ideario pasó a la generación del rap.

refs.q: P-Funk was and is more than a music style; it is a philosophy of life that for some approaches a religious creed.
refs.para: George Clinton and his P-Funk band developed something far greater than their simple identity as a musical ensemble. P-Funk was and is more than a music style; it is a philosophy of life that for some approaches a religious creed.
refs.chapter: Cap. 18: The Metaphysics of P: The Mothership Connection

refs.q: Without polemics, militarism, or racially charged code words, Clinton’s P-Funk placed the African-American sensibility at the center of the universe, and ultimately at the center of history.
refs.para: Bandleader George Clinton and writer-artist Pedro Bell were the primary sources of an endless flow of offbeat black philosophy that mocked the self-importance of religious and political doctrines while subtly creating their own. Clinton’s use of operatic vocals and church-based funk chants were common, but they became subversive when the lyrics reprised well-known themes in black religion, while affirming the present-day circumstances of blacks. On “Mothership Connection,” for example, the background vocal refrain “Swing down, sweet chariot/stop and let me ride” was a reference to the traditional black church hymn. “When Gabriel’s horn blow, you better be able to go” followed at the end of the song. In this case, however, the chariot was not an angel, but a spaceship with a funky black crew that had “returned to claim the pyramids.” Without polemics, militarism, or racially charged code words, Clinton’s P-Funk placed the African-American sensibility at the center of the universe, and ultimately at the center of history.
refs.chapter: Cap. 18: The Metaphysics of P: The Mothership Connection

refs.q: The Mothership was a celebration of the infinities of which blacks were now capable.
refs.para: The thunderous spectacle of lights, smoke, relentless music, and mystical symbolism was a profound example of black tradition in its unrestricted state. While the show was primarily designed as entertainment, and “Dr. Funkenstein” comes out of the ship to join the party, the landing of the Mothership serves as a metaphor for the “chariot” responsible for bringing “the chosen” to the Promised Land. The “chariot” is a myth, yet this chariot was real. The decade of the 1970s indeed represented that “Promised Land” of equality, a period of experiment in “integration” and “equality” for which the civil rights movement had worked for so long. P-Funk attempted to bring meaning and catharsis to that paradoxical realization of freedom. The Mothership was a celebration of the infinities of which blacks were now capable.
refs.chapter: Cap. 18: The Metaphysics of P: The Mothership Connection

refs.q: Thus the Rhythm of the One is the key to a collective spirit.
refs.para: The humanistic, inviting realm of many of the black bands of the 1970s consistently explored and advocated the idea of oneness, by maintaining large ensembles that could groove together, and by preaching songs of nondenominational spiritual and political unity. Their specific ideologies were often vague, but musically, most funk bands in the seventies had an implicit understanding of the groove, the essential funk lock. Funk bands accomplished rhythmically what few could say literally: that a diversity of rhythms represents a diversity of individuals, and that they all can be united—through the rhythmic groove of The Funk. Clinton’s P-Funk not only grooved harder, longer, and deeper than the rest; they codified the thematic trend into an all-encompassing concept: P-Funk. By expanding the unity amid diversity concept beyond the small band—to a large band—to an entire collective—a modern tribe—a community—or a universe—P-Funk music offers a symbolic basis of organizing a real community. This was the idea behind “One Nation Under a Groove.” Clinton described the impulse of his biggest hit “One Nation” as: “Everybody on the One, the whole world on the same pulse.” Thus the Rhythm of the One is the key to a collective spirit.
refs.chapter: Cap. 18: The Metaphysics of P: The Mothership Connection

refs.q: With The Funk, the sexual being and the spiritual being are one.
refs.para: At the center of the P-Funk worldview is an acceptance of the instinctive, sexual nature of the individual. With mock religious fervor, Clinton is prone to chanting: “All that is good, is nasty!” While this may seem offensive to some, the behavior of P-Funk members is not one of disrespect or negativity toward women or sex. Rather, as W. A. Brower put it, “P-Funk de-fetishizes an already demeaned subject.” With The Funk, the sexual being and the spiritual being are one.
refs.chapter: Cap. 18: The Metaphysics of P: The Mothership Connection
